How long will a power station run a laptop?

Power basics Updated 2026-08-08

Longer than almost anyone expects, because a laptop is a far smaller load than the wattage printed on its charger suggests. The US certified computer dataset puts short-idle power for a 13-to-16-inch notebook at 5.23 W across 1,016 models, and one manufacturer’s own measurement of a current 14-inch machine, display on, is 3.91 W.

At that size the power station’s own housekeeping becomes the larger half of the drain. The biggest machine here states a self-consumption of 10 W against the laptop’s 5.23 W, so 66% of what leaves the battery is the box keeping itself switched on — and it still runs the laptop for 104 h.

Open the runtime calculator →

The charger’s wattage is not the laptop’s wattage

The number most people reach for is the one moulded into the power brick. That figure describes how fast the charger can refill a flat battery — a peak capability, not a steady draw — and the record’s own distribution note makes the same point. A notebook doing ordinary work with its own battery already full sits in the single digits of watts, and the certified dataset below is measured rather than rated.

What a notebook actually draws

Two independent measurements of the same class of machine: a federal certification dataset covering a thousand models, and one manufacturer’s published environmental report for a specific one.

13–16-inch notebook — short idle 5.2 W Official spec · verified 2026-08-01 · high confidence

The mean across 1,016 certified models. Individual machines in the same set run from 0.2 W to 12.6 W.

One 14-inch machine — idle, display on 3.9 W Official spec · verified 2026-08-01 · high confidence

Asleep 0.2 W Official spec · verified 2026-08-01 · high confidence

Roughly one part in twenty of the running figure, and far under any power station’s own idle draw.

Official spec · verified 2026-08-01 · laptop record · certified dataset + manufacturer report

Below about ten watts, the power station is the load

Runtime on this site is usable capacity divided by the load plus the machine’s own self-consumption, because that is the form BLUETTI’s manual states its runtime formula in. For a kettle or a heater the second term is a rounding correction. For a laptop it is most of the denominator: 10 W of self-consumption against 5.23 W of laptop is 66% of the drain going nowhere near the computer. It is also why a runtime worked out as capacity divided by the load alone is not merely optimistic at this size — it is roughly three times too long.

A notebook on two machines, computed on this build

Both are trivially inside continuous output; the load-ratio column gives that away. What the two rows are really showing is how little of a battery a laptop consumes once nothing else is plugged in.

Which is why self-consumption is worth asking about

Only 10 of the 29 station records in this library carry the full set a runtime needs — depth of discharge and inverter efficiency alongside self-consumption — and that is exactly why those are the only records this site will print an hour figure for. For a small load the term dominates the answer, so a runtime quoted without it is not a slightly different number. It is a different question.

The 5,750 VA on the record, and why no verdict turns on it

Cold-start inrush, from an adapter data sheet

A switching power supply charges its input capacitors the instant it is plugged in. It is a real event with a real published figure, and it decides nothing here.

Inrush, as a multiple of input current 25 × Official spec · verified 2026-08-01 · medium confidence

From a third-party 65 W adapter’s own specification rather than a notebook maker’s. The counter-intuitive part: peak inrush barely scales with the size of the supply, so the smallest devices carry the highest multiples.

See the record →
The same event in volt-amperes 5,750 VA Official spec · verified 2026-08-01 · low confidence

Peak current times nominal voltage, over about 50 ms.

Official spec · verified 2026-08-01 · laptop record · 65 W adapter data sheet

A power station’s surge rating describes what it will hold for seconds. This is a capacitive spike two orders of magnitude shorter, so the two figures share a unit and describe different things — comparing them would refuse pairings that work perfectly well. Our engine therefore treats this one as advisory: it is on the record, it is dated, and it never decides a verdict. Where it does become practical advice is a strip of chargers switched on together, because the spikes add and a machine can trip on nothing but being plugged in.

Questions people ask

How many watts does a laptop use?
Far less than its charger is rated for. The US certified computer dataset puts short-idle power for 13-to-16-inch notebooks at 5.23 W across 1,016 models, with individual machines from 0.2 W to 12.6 W, and one manufacturer’s own report measures a current 14-inch machine at 3.91 W with the display on. The wattage printed on the power brick describes how fast it can refill a flat battery, not what the computer draws.
How long will a power station run a laptop?
On the records here that state both usable capacity and self-consumption, 17 hours from a 300 Wh class machine and 104 hours from a 2,000 Wh class one. Those hours divide by the laptop plus the power station’s own idle draw, which at this size is the larger of the two terms — capacity divided by the laptop alone would overstate the answer by roughly three times.
Will plugging a laptop charger in trip a power station?
On its own, no. A 65 W adapter data sheet states a cold-start peak of under 50 A at 115 V, about 25 times its running current, but it lasts on the order of 50 ms — far shorter than the seconds a station’s surge rating describes, which is why our engine records it and never decides a verdict on it. Several chargers switched on at the same instant is the case worth avoiding.
